hypothesis: A pairwise Elo/Bradley-Terry tournament of the kind used by AI co-scientist produces winners that look just as decisive in target-absent pools (no correct candidate) as in target-present pools, so tournament statistics carry almost no signal that the pool contains no correct answer.
gap_with_citations: AI co-scientist (Gottweis et al., arXiv 2502.18864; verified this session via WebSearch summaries, arxiv.org direct fetch blocked) ranks hypotheses with an Elo tournament (initial Elo 1200, pairwise, often debate-style matches) and validates it by correlating Elo with correctness. That validation is on pools where correct answers exist. The search turned up no test of the tournament on all-wrong pools. Our corpus lineup work (corpus/02-lineup-problem-verifier/frontier-run/paper.md; corpus/08-hypothesis-lineup-pilot/FINDING.md) shows accept/PICK judges choose a wrong answer in about 70 percent of target-absent pools, but it never tested a forced-choice pairwise tournament, where NONE is not even an option. The novelty audit (corpus/10-novelty-audit/00-SUMMARY.md) notes that co-scientist and Robin rankers are validated only on target-present pools. 2608.17270 (from corpus, not re-verified) could add target-absent pools in v2.
prediction: On real CRUXEval-O wrong outputs, a tournament statistic (top BT strength margin over second place, or the top candidate's win rate) separates target-absent from target-present pools with AUROC <= 0.65. In at least 50 percent of target-absent pools, the top candidate wins at least 80 percent of its matches.
kill_criterion: Kill if the AUROC of the best pre-specified tournament statistic (top-1 win rate) for absent vs present is >= 0.75 (95 percent bootstrap CI lower bound >= 0.65), or if fewer than 30 percent of absent pools produce a top candidate with win rate >= 0.8.
smallest_experiment: Items: 40 CRUXEval-O functions (git clone facebookresearch/cruxeval; gold by executing Python) with >= 5 distinct real wrong outputs, collected from haiku sampled at several personas (about 800 haiku generation calls). Pools of 6: ABSENT = 6 wrong; PRESENT = gold + 5 of the same wrongs. Arms: full round robin (15 pairwise matches per pool, judge = haiku, forced A/B like co-scientist, side randomized), plus an ISO arm where the tournament winner is judged alone (accept/reject). Calls: 40 x 2 x 15 = 1200 haiku match calls + 80 ISO calls + about 800 generation calls = about 2100 haiku. Optional: 40 sonnet matches on 4 pools as a tier check.
why_it_matters: Co-scientist-style systems present the top-Elo hypothesis as the best candidate. If the tournament cannot tell 'best of a bad set' from 'right', the reported Elo gains over time say nothing about whether any candidate is correct, and a cheap absolute check of the winner (ISO arm) is the fix.
scoop_risk: Medium. The lineup bridge itself is ours (corpus). 2608.17270 v2 and groups reimplementing open co-scientist could add an all-wrong control at any time.

hypothesis: Elo tournaments assume a stable, near-transitive latent quality order. Among all-wrong candidates that order does not exist: preference cycles are much more common and the identity of the winner depends on match order and position, so the 'best hypothesis' in a target-absent pool is largely arbitrary.
gap_with_citations: Xu, Ruis, Rocktaschel, Kirk, 'Investigating Non-Transitivity in LLM-as-a-Judge' (arXiv 2502.14074, ICML 2025; verified this session) find non-transitivity in AlpacaEval and propose round-robin BT. 'Elo Uncovered' (arXiv 2311.17295, GEM 2023; verified this session) finds Elo sensitive to match-order permutation, especially when competitors are closely matched. AI co-scientist (2502.18864; verified this session) assumes Elo is a good proxy for relative ranking and schedules matches non-uniformly (similar, newer and top hypotheses first). No one has conditioned intransitivity or winner stability on whether a correct candidate is present.
prediction: The share of intransitive triads (3-cycles, with order-swapped verdicts aggregated) in ABSENT pools is >= 2x that in PRESENT pools. Top-1 agreement between two independent tournaments over the same pool (different random match order and sides, sequential Elo update with K=32) is <= 0.5 in ABSENT pools and >= 0.8 in PRESENT pools.
kill_criterion: Kill if the ABSENT/PRESENT ratio of the 3-cycle rate is < 1.5 (or its bootstrap CI includes 1.0), or if the ABSENT top-1 agreement is >= 0.7.
smallest_experiment: Reuses the U1 pools and matches. Adds a second full pass with sides swapped (1200 more haiku calls) so that each pair has 2 verdicts. Triads are computed from the round robin; two sequential-Elo replays use independent seeds over the logged verdicts plus 2 x 40 x 2 fresh Swiss-style schedules (about 300 more calls). Total about 1500 haiku calls beyond U1.
why_it_matters: If the winner of an all-wrong pool is a coin flip over match order, then co-scientist's 'Elo rises over iterations' can come from scheduling alone, and order-swap consistency becomes a usable signal of target absence.
scoop_risk: Medium-low. The non-transitivity literature (2502.14074) is active but frames the problem as position bias over model rankings, not as correct-candidate absence.

hypothesis: Debate assumes one debater holds the truth. When both debaters defend different wrong answers and the judge may answer NEITHER, a weak judge still endorses one side most of the time, and it does so more often than it accepts the same wrong answer in consultancy. In the both-wrong regime, debate increases false endorsement.
gap_with_citations: Khan et al., 'Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers' (arXiv 2402.06782, ICML 2024; verified this session) and Kenton et al., 'On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs' (arXiv 2407.04622, NeurIPS 2024; verified this session) give the judge two answers, one of them correct, or let debaters choose their sides between the options. The search found no protocol with a both-wrong condition and a NEITHER option (this session's search: 'nothing addresses a neither or abstain option where both debaters argue incorrect answers'). 2409.00113 (from corpus) covers MCQ abstention without debate.
prediction: Arm BW (wrong vs wrong debate, NEITHER allowed): the judge picks a side in >= 60 percent of items. Arm CW (consultancy for one of those same wrong answers, judge accept/reject): false accept <= 40 percent. Paired difference BW - CW >= +15 points. Arm CR (correct vs wrong debate) reproduces the standard debate benefit, with judge accuracy above CW's correct-rejection baseline.
kill_criterion: Kill if the BW side-pick rate is <= CW false-accept + 5 points (paired, item level), or if the BW side-pick rate is < 30 percent.
smallest_experiment: Items: 60 CRUXEval-O functions with >= 2 distinct real wrong outputs. Debaters: sonnet, assigned answers, one opening argument plus one rebuttal each. Judge: haiku, no chain of thought, sees the code and the arguments, answers A/B/NEITHER; 3 independent judge samples. Arms: CR, BW, CW (consultant sonnet, 2 turns). Calls: sonnet 60 x (4 + 4 + 2) = 600, which can be trimmed to 1 turn each to give 300; haiku judges 60 x 3 arms x 3 = 540.
why_it_matters: Debate is proposed for questions humans cannot answer, which are exactly the questions where neither proposed answer may be right. If debate hides target absence that consultancy would reveal, the protocol ranking reverses in that regime.
scoop_risk: Medium. It is an obvious extension for the debate groups (Khan, Kenton, Michael) but appears unclaimed as of this session's search.

hypothesis: Aggregating verifier calls (k samples of one judge, or a panel across tiers) assumes false accepts are roughly independent given the candidate. In fact they concentrate on a small set of 'convincing' wrong candidates, so majority-of-k false accept falls far less than the binomial prediction and cross-tier panels share their false accepts.
gap_with_citations: PoLL, Verga et al., 'Replacing Judges with Juries' (arXiv 2404.18796; verified this session) argues that a panel of diverse models reduces intra-model bias. Weaver (arXiv 2506.18203, NeurIPS 2025; verified this session) combines weak verifiers with Snorkel-style weak supervision, estimating accuracies from pairwise statistics. Such latent-variable estimators usually assume conditional independence, but this session could not confirm the exact assumption from abstracts, so this is flagged as an inference. Zhao et al. (arXiv 2502.01839; verified this session) scale verification by repeated sampling. The novelty audit marks solver-side co-failure as preempted (2606.27288, 2606.02646; from corpus); the gap is on the verifier side, measured per candidate.
prediction: On real CRUXEval-O wrong outputs, false accept under haiku majority-of-5 is >= 3x the binomial prediction from the mean single-call f. At least 60 percent of all false-accept verdicts fall on <= 20 percent of wrong candidates. P(sonnet false-accepts | haiku majority false-accepts) >= 3x P(sonnet false-accepts).
kill_criterion: Kill if the observed/predicted majority-of-5 false-accept ratio has a bootstrap CI lower bound < 1.5, and the sonnet conditional lift is < 2.
smallest_experiment: Items: CRUXEval-O. Candidates: 200 real wrong + 100 correct outputs (from the haiku generation pass in U1). Arms: haiku ISO accept/reject x 5 independent calls (1500 haiku); sonnet ISO x 1 on all 300 (300 sonnet). Analysis: ICC, majority-k curve vs binomial, cross-tier conditional lift, candidate-level clustering bootstrap.
why_it_matters: Every 'more verifier compute' or 'jury' result implicitly prices verifier calls as independent evidence. If errors are candidate-driven, then extra samples or extra tiers buy little exactly on the dangerous candidates, and selection-law ceilings (Stroebl et al., arXiv 2411.17501; verified this session) must be computed with a correlated f.
scoop_risk: Medium-high. Correlated judge errors are discussed widely; the explicit majority-of-k-vs-binomial measurement on real errors is a small, quickly scoopable step.

hypothesis: Weak-judge oversight assumes the judge's false-accept rate is a property of the judge (and the task). It is also a property of who produced the error: on the same item, wrong answers produced by a stronger model are accepted by a weak judge substantially more often than wrong answers produced by a weaker model.
gap_with_citations: Kenton et al. (arXiv 2407.04622; verified this session) report that stronger debaters raise judge accuracy, but they measure protocol accuracy, not false accept conditioned on error source with the item held fixed. Selection-law work (Stroebl et al., arXiv 2411.17501; verified this session; lineup paper section 1 lists more from corpus) treats f as constant across generators. This session's search found no study that cross-tabulates judge false-positive rate by the capability of the generator, only indirect hints that stronger models' residual errors are 'more plausible' (arXiv 2609.06149, surfaced by search, not opened).
prediction: Within item (items where haiku and sonnet both err, with different wrong outputs), haiku-judge false accept of sonnet-authored wrongs is >= 1.5x that of haiku-authored wrongs in the answer-plus-rationale format. In an answer-only arm the ratio drops below 1.3, which locates the effect in the rationale.
kill_criterion: Kill if the paired ratio FA(sonnet-wrong)/FA(haiku-wrong) in the rationale arm is < 1.2, or its item-clustered bootstrap CI includes 1.0.
smallest_experiment: Items: run sonnet on the 300 CRUXEval-O items hardest for haiku (300 sonnet calls) and keep the about 60 or more where both err with different outputs. Rationales are capped at 3 sentences in both sources. Arms: rationale vs answer-only. Judge: haiku ISO, 3 samples. Calls: haiku 60 x 2 sources x 2 arms x 3 = 720 + generation (reused from U1); sonnet 300.
why_it_matters: Scalable oversight scales the overseen model's strength. If the overseer's false accept grows with the strength of the overseen model, then oversight error budgets measured on today's generators are optimistic for tomorrow's, which is the central failure the field worries about, here in measured form.
scoop_risk: Medium. It is natural for weak-to-strong and judge-robustness groups, and appears unclaimed in this session's search.

hypothesis: Generate-until-accepted loops and sequential verification assume each verdict is independent of earlier verdicts. They are not: after a run of rejections on the same problem, an LLM judge becomes more lenient (a quota effect), so the false accept of a fixed wrong candidate rises with the number of prior rejections shown in context.
gap_with_citations: The lineup paper (corpus) shows that serial in-prompt presentation gives a low false accept (0.012), the best mitigation it found, but it never tested whether that rate depends on serial position or on prior verdicts. Position bias within a single prompt is well documented (arXiv 2406.07791; from corpus, surfaced again in this session's search). This session's search found no study of acceptance as a function of the judge's own prior rejections. Zhao et al. (arXiv 2502.01839; verified this session) and co-scientist reflection loops verify candidates repeatedly on the same problem.
prediction: For a fixed wrong candidate, haiku false accept with 6 prior REJECT verdicts in context (on other real wrong candidates for the same item) is >= 2x the rate with 0 prior verdicts. With 6 prior ACCEPT verdicts it is lower than the 0 condition (a contrast effect). The trend over k in {0, 3, 6} is monotone.
kill_criterion: Kill if FA(k=6 rejects)/FA(k=0) < 1.3, or the Cochran-Armitage trend test over k in {0, 3, 6} rejects gives p > 0.05.
smallest_experiment: Items: CRUXEval-O. Targets: 150 real wrong + 50 correct candidates. The history is rendered in the prompt as the judge's own earlier verdicts on other candidates for that item (real wrongs, verdicts fixed by condition). Conditions: k=0, k=3 rejects, k=6 rejects, k=6 accepts. 2 samples each. Calls: 200 x 4 x 2 = 1600 haiku. Bonus at zero cost: re-analyze the serial_8 arm of the lineup run by slot position, if the raw data are available.
why_it_matters: Retry-until-verified pipelines stop at the first accept. If leniency builds with each rejection, the false accept at the stopping time is far above the per-call f used to justify the loop, and the fix is simply to verify each candidate in a fresh context.
scoop_risk: Low-medium. Order effects are studied, but not verdict-history-induced leniency in accept/reject verifiers.

hypothesis: Debate stopping rules and confidence estimates treat agent agreement as evidence of correctness. Debate itself destroys that evidence: the AUROC of agreement for predicting correctness is lower after debate rounds than at round 0, because debate converts informative disagreement into unanimity, including unanimous wrong answers.
gap_with_citations: Du et al. (ICML 2024; from corpus) use convergence and consensus as the debate outcome. Morandi (arXiv 2605.19193; from corpus, not re-verified) uses sequential stopping for debate and reports that calibration collapses on MMLU. Wu et al. (arXiv 2511.07784; from corpus) report that majority pressure suppresses correction. 'Debate or Vote' (arXiv 2508.17536; from corpus) attributes most gains to voting. No one in the corpus or this session's search compares agreement-as-confidence AUROC before vs after debate on the same items.
prediction: On 150 CRUXEval-O items in the haiku 40 to 70 percent accuracy band (3 haiku agents, 2 debate rounds), the AUROC of the final-majority agreement fraction for correctness drops by >= 0.05 from round 0 to round 2. Among items with initial disagreement, the unanimous-wrong rate at round 2 is >= 2x that at round 0.
kill_criterion: Kill if AUROC(round 2) >= AUROC(round 0) - 0.01 (paired bootstrap), or if the unanimous-wrong ratio is < 1.3.
smallest_experiment: Items: 150 CRUXEval-O. Arms: 3-agent haiku debate x 2 rounds (450 + 900 = 1350 haiku calls). Control: 3 extra independent samples per item instead of a debate round (450 haiku), to separate 'more samples' from 'interaction'. Total about 1800 haiku.
why_it_matters: Adaptive-compute MAS (stop when agents agree) and debate-as-verifier pipelines rely on post-debate agreement as a confidence score. If debate degrades that signal, these systems are confidently wrong on exactly the items where debate was supposed to help.
scoop_risk: Medium. The debate-dynamics literature is crowded (see novelty audit B-line), but the before/after AUROC framing is a clean, unclaimed measurement.
